terms.grammar: preposition with the ablative; written after the pronouns: mēcum, tēcum, sēcum, nōbīscum, vōbīscum
evidence: Sen. Ep. 55.11: mēcum studē, mēcum cēnā, mēcum ambulā
Hor. Ep. 1.7.70: sī cēnās hodiē mēcum
terms.comment: Of the people one is with, and of things one has with one (cum clāvī, with the key). Not of a tool: “with a knife” is the plain ablative (see “with”, the tool). Of manner, magnā cum cūrā, though an adverb is often plainer (dīligenter).

evidence: Ter. Ph. 556: ūnā tēcum bona mala tolerābimus
terms.comment: Stresses the being together; see together.

phrases.latin: itaque mēcum studē, mēcum cēnā, mēcum ambulā
phrases.english: so study with me, dine with me, walk with me

phrases.latin: sīc ignōvisse putātō mē tibi, sī cēnās hodiē mēcum. — ut libet
phrases.english: consider yourself forgiven, if you dine with me today. — As you like.

phrases.latin: Nōlī metuere: ūnā tēcum bona mala tolerābimus.
phrases.english: Don’t be afraid: we’ll bear the good and the bad together with you.

phrases.latin: jamdūdum in vīllā sedēns exspectō cum clāvī tē … — em quīn adsum, veniō ad līmen, forēs aperī
phrases.english: I’ve been sitting in the house with the key waiting for you for ages … — Here I am, I’m coming to the door, open up!

sources: Lewis & Short: cum · Lewis & Short: una
